item.title: CK Skills Vulnerability Mining Agent: Complete Guide to SRC Bug Hunting with Claude Code and Codex (2026)
item.description: Learn how to use CK skills vulnerability mining agents with Claude Code and Codex CLI. Step-by-step guide to installing, configuring, and running SRC bug hunting skill bundles.
item.content:encoded:
A CK skills vulnerability mining agent transforms Claude Code or Codex CLI from a general-purpose coding assistant into a specialized SRC (Security Response Center) bug hunter by loading reusable skill files that encode real-world vulnerability detection patterns, recon methodology, and reporting templates. These skill bundles — like Claude-BugHunter with 82 skills curated from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports — give AI coding agents the ability to systematically discover SQL injection, XSS, SSRF, IDOR, and 20+ other vulnerability classes across web applications, APIs, and smart contracts without requiring the user to re-prompt methodology every session.

What Are Agent Skills and Why Use Them for Vulnerability Mining?

Agent skills are reusable instruction files — written in the SKILL.md format with YAML frontmatter and Markdown body — that teach an AI coding agent how to perform a specific task. For vulnerability mining, a skill might contain the exact methodology for detecting blind SQL injection, the payload patterns for testing SSTI, or the recon steps for discovering hidden API endpoints. Instead of describing your approach to the agent each time, you load a skill bundle once and the agent knows the full playbook.

The key advantage is consistency. A human bug bounty hunter develops their methodology over years of trial and error. Agent skills encode that hard-won knowledge into a format the AI can execute reliably every session. Claude-BugHunter, for example, distills patterns from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports into 82 executable skills — every session starts with the same high-quality methodology regardless of the hunter’s experience level.

For SRC (Security Response Center) platforms — which are particularly popular in China and operated by companies like Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei — vulnerability mining agents with CK skills can automate the repetitive recon and detection phases while the human focuses on exploit validation and report writing.

The Agent Skills Open Standard (agentskills.io) and Multi-Harness Compatibility

In December 2025, the agent skills ecosystem reached a major milestone: the agentskills.io open standard was published, defining a universal SKILL.md format that works across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent, Gemini CLI, and OpenClaw. A skill written for one platform runs on all of them without modification.

This is a game-changer for vulnerability researchers. Previously, a bug hunter using Claude Code would need a different skill format than someone using Codex CLI. Now, the same Claude-BugHunter skill bundle that teaches your Claude Code session to detect SSRF also works when you switch to Codex CLI for a different project. The skill file is just a Markdown document with structured frontmatter — no platform-specific code, no per-harness rewrites.

The standard defines three key components:

  • SKILL.md: The main file with YAML frontmatter (name, description, tags) and the instruction body
  • references/: Optional directory for supporting data files, payload lists, or configuration templates
  • scripts/: Optional directory for executable scripts the skill may invoke

This simplicity is what drove adoption. By mid-2026, the agentskills.io registry hosts thousands of skills across security, DevOps, data science, and creative domains.

Progressive Disclosure — How Skills Load Without Wasting Tokens

One concern with loading large skill bundles is token consumption. A bundle like Claude-BugHunter with 82 skills could easily consume 50,000+ tokens if every skill loaded at session start. The agent skills standard solves this with progressive disclosure.

At session initialization, only each skill’s name and description — roughly 100 tokens per skill — are loaded into the agent’s context. The full instruction body, methodology, payload lists, and detection patterns load only when the agent determines the skill is relevant to the current task. If you’re testing for XSS, the XSS detection skill loads in full while the SSRF and IDOR skills remain as lightweight stubs.

This architecture makes it practical to maintain skill bundles with dozens or even hundreds of skills. Claude-BugHunter’s 82 skills consume roughly 8,200 tokens at session start — well within the context window of any modern model — while the full skill content (potentially 200,000+ tokens across all skills) is loaded on demand.

For vulnerability mining, this means you can have a comprehensive skill library covering every vulnerability class without paying the token cost for skills you aren’t using in the current session.

Top Vulnerability Mining Skill Bundles for Claude Code and Codex

The ecosystem has produced several mature skill bundles specifically designed for vulnerability mining and bug bounty hunting. Here is a comparison of the leading options:

Bundle Skills/Agents Vulnerability Classes Key Feature Platforms
Claude-BugHunter 82 skills, 15 slash commands 24 classes (SQLi, XSS, SSRF, LFI, RCE, IDOR, SSTI, etc.) 681 HackerOne report patterns Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode
BountyForge Dual-agent toolkit Web2, mobile, Web3 smart contracts Shared skills across Codex + Claude Code Codex CLI, Claude Code
Argus Multi-agent (LATS+MCTS) SQLi, XSS, SSRF, LFI, RCE, IDOR, SSTI, auth bypass, info disclosure MCTS intelligent vulnerability exploration Docker Compose (9 containers)
Pentest Agent Suite 50 agents, 26 slash commands Web, network, cloud, mobile 19 CLI tools, 7 platform support Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Continue

Claude-BugHunter — 82 Skills for Bug Hunting and Red-Team

Claude-BugHunter is the most comprehensive vulnerability mining skill bundle available. Its 82 skills are organized into four operational layers:

  1. Think — Methodology skills that guide the agent’s approach to different vulnerability classes
  2. Hunt webapps — 48 hunt-* skills covering specific attack surfaces (hunt-sqli, hunt-xss, hunt-ssrf, hunt-idor, etc.)
  3. Hit the perimeter — Enterprise attack chain skills for chaining multiple vulnerabilities
  4. Ship it — Triage, validation, and reporting skills with VRT-aware templates

The bundle includes Burp MCP integration, meaning the agent can interact with Burp Suite’s proxy, scanner, and repeater through the Model Context Protocol. This bridges the gap between AI-driven analysis and industry-standard web security testing tools.

Installation is straightforward. Claude-BugHunter supports two methods:

Plugin install (recommended):

claude plugins install claude-bughunter

Copy install (for Codex CLI or manual setup):

git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git
cp -r Claude-BugHunter/skills/* ~/.claude/skills/

BountyForge — Dual-Agent Bug Bounty Toolkit

BountyForge takes a different approach by providing a dual-agent setup that works across both Codex CLI and Claude Code. It includes shared skills, commands, agents, and rules files that both platforms can use.

The toolkit covers three major attack surfaces:

  • Web2 recon — Subdomain enumeration, endpoint discovery, parameter fuzzing
  • Mobile static/dynamic analysis — APK decompilation, traffic interception, insecure storage checks
  • Web3 smart contract audit — Solidity vulnerability patterns, reentrancy detection, access control analysis

BountyForge’s install script automatically sets up both platforms plus runtime tools (subfinder, httpx, nuclei, katana, ffuf) in a single command:

git clone https://github.com/0x1Jar/BountyForge.git
cd BountyForge
chmod +x install.sh && ./install.sh

The workflow follows a structured 5-phase approach: recon → map → hunt → validate → report, with a 7-Question Gate at each phase to ensure quality.

Argus — AI-Powered SRC Multi-Agent System (LATS + MCTS)

Argus represents the cutting edge of AI-driven vulnerability mining. It uses a hybrid LATS (Language Agent Tree Search) + ReAct architecture with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for intelligent exploration of the vulnerability space.

Unlike simpler skill bundles that follow linear detection patterns, Argus actively explores the attack surface. The MCTS algorithm simulates thousands of potential attack paths, evaluates their likelihood of success, and prioritizes the most promising ones. This is particularly effective for SRC platforms where the attack surface is large and the reward structure favors finding high-impact vulnerabilities.

Argus integrates 16 security tools:

  • Katana — API endpoint discovery and crawling
  • Playwright — Browser automation for DOM-based testing
  • mitmproxy — Traffic capture and manipulation
  • crawlergo — Deep crawling for hidden endpoints
  • PoC sandbox — Safe proof-of-concept execution

Deployment uses Docker Compose with 9 containers, making it the most resource-intensive option but also the most capable for automated SRC mining:

git clone https://github.com/R0x7e/Argus.git
cd Argus
docker-compose up -d

Pentest Agent Suite — 50 Specialized Security Agents

Pentest Agent Suite delivers 50 specialized security agents with 26 slash commands and 19 CLI tools. It supports 7 major AI coding platforms: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, and Continue.

Each agent is a specialized skill focused on a specific security domain — web application testing, network penetration testing, cloud security assessment, and mobile application analysis. The suite’s strength is breadth: it covers the full penetration testing lifecycle rather than focusing solely on web vulnerability mining.

Step-by-Step: Installing Agent Skills for Vulnerability Mining

The installation process varies slightly depending on your platform and the skill bundle you choose. Here are the most common installation paths.

Installing Claude-BugHunter (Plugin vs Copy Install)

For Claude Code (plugin method):

# Install the plugin
claude plugins install claude-bughunter

# Verify installation
claude plugins list

For Codex CLI or manual setup (copy method):

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git

# Copy skills to your agent's skills directory
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/
cp -r Claude-BugHunter/skills/* ~/.claude/skills/

# For Codex CLI
mkdir -p ~/.codex/skills/
cp -r Claude-BugHunter/skills/* ~/.codex/skills/

Installing BountyForge for Codex and Claude Code

BountyForge’s unified install script handles both platforms:

git clone https://github.com/0x1Jar/BountyForge.git
cd BountyForge
chmod +x install.sh
./install.sh

The script installs skills to both ~/.claude/skills/ and ~/.codex/skills/ directories, plus downloads runtime tools (subfinder, httpx, nuclei, katana, ffuf) to your PATH.

Cross-Platform Install with –all Flag

Some skill bundles now support a unified install command that targets all detected platforms:

# Install a skill bundle across all available platforms
agentskills install claude-bughunter --all

This command detects which AI coding platforms are installed on your system and installs the skills to each one’s skills directory. It’s the simplest way to maintain a consistent skill library across your development environment.

Connecting to Security Tools via MCP (Burp Suite Integration)

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the bridge between AI coding agents and external security tools. For vulnerability mining, the most important integration is with Burp Suite — the industry-standard web security testing platform.

Claude-BugHunter includes built-in Burp MCP integration that allows the agent to:

  • Send requests through Burp’s proxy for traffic inspection
  • Feed discovered endpoints to Burp Scanner for automated scanning
  • Use Burp Repeater to manually test parameter variations
  • Import Burp project files for collaborative analysis

Setting up the MCP connection requires a Burp MCP server running alongside your AI coding agent:

# Install the Burp MCP server
pip install burp-mcp-server

# Start the server (Burp Suite must be running)
burp-mcp-server --port 8081

Then configure your agent to use the MCP server by adding it to your CLAUDE.md or agent configuration:

mcp_servers:
  burp:
    url: http://localhost:8081
    transport: sse

BountyForge also supports Burp MCP integration, along with other security tools through its extensible tool integration layer.

Skill Safety — Scanning Skills Before Installation

The rapid growth of the agent skills ecosystem has attracted security researchers — and unfortunately, malicious actors. Before installing any skill bundle, you should scan it for security issues.

NVIDIA SkillSpector — 64 Vulnerability Patterns

NVIDIA open-sourced SkillSpector in early 2026, a tool that scans agent skills for 64 vulnerability patterns across 16 categories. In their analysis of the skills ecosystem, SkillSpector found that 26.1% of skills contain at least one vulnerability — ranging from prompt injection vectors to dangerous code execution patterns.

# Install SkillSpector
pip install skillspector

# Scan a skill bundle
skillspector scan ~/.claude/skills/ --format sarif --output results.sarif

Snyk ToxicSkills — 36% of Skills Have Security Flaws

Snyk’s ToxicSkills audit (February 2026) examined 3,984 skills from public registries and found:

  • 36% (1,467 skills) had at least one security flaw
  • 13.4% (534 skills) had critical issues
  • 76 human-confirmed malicious payloads designed to exfiltrate data or execute unauthorized commands

These numbers underscore the importance of treating skills like any other software dependency. You wouldn’t install a random npm package without reviewing it — the same caution applies to agent skills.

Cisco Skill Scanner — SARIF/HTML/JSON Output

Cisco released a skill scanner that produces output in SARIF, HTML, and JSON formats, making it easy to integrate into CI/CD pipelines:

# Install Cisco Skill Scanner
pip install cisco-skill-scanner

# Scan and generate HTML report
cisco-skill-scan ~/.claude/skills/ --format html --output report.html

Best practice: Always scan new skill bundles in an isolated environment before adding them to your production agent configuration. Use a sandboxed agent session to verify the skills behave as expected.

Building Your Own Vulnerability Mining Skill (SKILL.md Format)

Creating a custom vulnerability mining skill is straightforward. The SKILL.md format requires YAML frontmatter and a Markdown body:

---
name: hunt-ssrf-detection
description: Detect Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerabilities in web applications
tags:
  - ssrf
  - server-side-request-forgery
  - web-security
  - vulnerability-detection
---

# SSRF Detection Methodology

## Reconnaissance
1. Identify features that fetch external resources (URL inputs, file imports, webhooks)
2. Look for parameters: `url=`, `path=`, `file=`, `redirect=`, `src=`, `target=`
3. Test with a collaborator/request-bin service

## Detection Payloads
- `http://[your-collaborator].burpcollaborator.net/ssrf-test`
- `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` (AWS metadata)
- `http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin`
- `file:///etc/passwd`

## Blind SSRF Detection
- Use DNS-based out-of-band detection
- Monitor collaborator for DNS lookups and HTTP callbacks
- Time-based detection: delay payloads with `?sleep=10`

## Validation
- Confirm the source IP of the callback is the target server
- Test for cloud metadata access (AWS, GCP, Azure)
- Document the full request chain

Save this file as hunt-ssrf-detection.skill.md in your skills directory. The agent will automatically discover it on the next session start.

For more complex skills, you can include a references/ directory with payload lists and a scripts/ directory with automation scripts.

Best Practices for AI-Assisted Bug Bounty Hunting

Workflow: Recon → Map → Hunt → Validate → Report

The most effective bug bounty hunters using AI agents follow a structured workflow:

  1. Recon — Use agent skills to discover subdomains, endpoints, and attack surface. Tools like subfinder and httpx are invoked through skill scripts.
  2. Map — The agent maps the application architecture, identifies authentication mechanisms, and documents API endpoints.
  3. Hunt — Load vulnerability-specific skills (hunt-sqli, hunt-xss, hunt-ssrf) and systematically test each attack surface.
  4. Validate — The agent presents findings with evidence. The human verifies exploitability.
  5. Report — Use reporting skills to generate VRT-compliant vulnerability reports with reproducible steps.

The Validation Gap — When to Trust the Agent vs Verify Manually

Claude Code and Codex CLI excel at recon and source-code review but consistently need human validation for the “last mile” of exploit proof. This is not a limitation to work around — it is a feature of an effective human-AI partnership.

Trust the agent for:

  • Subdomain enumeration and endpoint discovery
  • Parameter fuzzing and payload delivery
  • Source code review for common vulnerability patterns
  • Initial triage and severity estimation

Verify manually for:

  • Exploit proof-of-concept construction
  • Business logic vulnerabilities
  • Authentication bypass chains
  • Impact assessment in the application context

Model Selection Strategy

Different models excel at different phases of vulnerability mining:

Phase Recommended Model Rationale
Recon and discovery Claude Haiku or GPT-4o-mini High throughput, low cost for volume work
Vulnerability analysis Claude Sonnet or GPT-4o Strong reasoning, good at pattern matching
Exploit development Claude Opus or o1 Deep reasoning, chain-of-thought for complex exploits
Report writing Claude Sonnet Balanced quality and speed for structured output

SRC-Specific Workflows with Multi-Agent Systems

SRC (Security Response Center) platforms have unique requirements that make multi-agent systems particularly effective. Unlike traditional bug bounty programs, SRC platforms often:

  • Have specific scope definitions and testing guidelines
  • Require vulnerability reports in a specific format
  • Operate on a points-and-rankings system
  • Cover a wide range of products and services

Argus’s multi-agent architecture addresses these requirements through its LATS + MCTS approach. The system deploys multiple specialized agents:

  • Recon Agent — Discovers attack surface and maps endpoints
  • Analysis Agent — Tests for vulnerabilities using MCTS-guided exploration
  • Validation Agent — Confirms findings and eliminates false positives
  • Report Agent — Generates SRC-compliant vulnerability reports

The MCTS component is particularly valuable for SRC mining. Instead of testing vulnerabilities in a fixed order, the system explores the attack space intelligently — prioritizing high-value targets, chaining low-severity issues into critical exploits, and adapting its strategy based on findings.

For Chinese SRC platforms (Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei, ByteDance), Argus includes specific skill modules that understand the platform’s scope rules, reward structure, and reporting format.

Conclusion — Building Your Vulnerability Mining Agent Skill System

The CK skills vulnerability mining agent ecosystem has matured rapidly. With the agentskills.io open standard ensuring cross-platform compatibility, progressive disclosure keeping token costs manageable, and bundles like Claude-BugHunter (82 skills), BountyForge (dual-agent toolkit), and Argus (LATS+MCTS multi-agent system) providing production-ready capabilities, there has never been a better time to build your vulnerability mining skill system.

Start with a single bundle — Claude-BugHunter is the most comprehensive for general web application testing. Install it, scan it with SkillSpector, and run your first recon session. As you gain confidence, add BountyForge for mobile and Web3 coverage, and consider Argus for automated SRC mining.

Remember the security-first approach: treat skills like code dependencies. Scan before installing, review before trusting, and always validate AI-discovered vulnerabilities manually before submitting reports. The agent is your force multiplier — your judgment is still the critical factor.

The future of bug bounty hunting is human-AI collaboration. The skills you build and install today will compound in value as the ecosystem grows and models improve. Start building your vulnerability mining agent skill system now.

FAQ

Q: What is a CK skills vulnerability mining agent? A: A CK skills vulnerability mining agent is an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Codex CLI) enhanced with reusable skill files that encode vulnerability detection patterns, recon methodology, and reporting templates for SRC bug hunting. These skills transform general-purpose coding agents into specialized security researchers.

Q: Which skill bundle is best for beginners? A: Claude-BugHunter is the best starting point for beginners. Its 82 skills cover 24 vulnerability classes with patterns from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports, and the four-layer organization (Think, Hunt webapps, Hit the perimeter, Ship it) provides a clear learning path from methodology to reporting.

Q: Are agent skills safe to install? A: Not all of them. Snyk’s ToxicSkills audit found 36% of marketplace skills have security flaws, and 76 confirmed malicious payloads were discovered. Always scan skill bundles with NVIDIA SkillSpector or Cisco Skill Scanner before installation, and test new skills in an isolated environment first.

Q: Can I use the same skills on both Claude Code and Codex CLI? A: Yes. The agentskills.io open standard (December 2025) ensures skills written in SKILL.md format work across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent, Gemini CLI, and OpenClaw without modification. The same skill file works on all platforms.

Q: How does progressive disclosure save tokens with large skill bundles? A: Progressive disclosure loads only each skill’s name and description (~100 tokens) at session start. The full skill content loads only when the agent determines the skill is relevant to the current task. This means a bundle with 82 skills consumes roughly 8,200 tokens at startup rather than 200,000+ tokens for full content.

item.title: OpenKritt AI Agent Vulnerability Hunting: Orchestrate AI Agents to Find Real Vulnerabilities in Code
item.description: OpenKritt is an open-source AI security research platform that orchestrates multi-agent workflows to find real code vulnerabilities, built by a team with $1.5M+ in bug bounty payouts.
item.content:encoded:
What is open·kritt?

Open·kritt is an open-source AI security research platform that orchestrates multiple AI agents to find real vulnerabilities in code. Released on July 20, 2026, it lets security researchers build custom workflows where each step — reconnaissance, scanning, validation, and reporting — is handled by a dedicated AI agent running in an isolated Docker container. Unlike monolithic vulnerability scanners that blast a target with generic checks, open·kritt breaks security research into focused, validated tasks that produce actionable findings with proof-of-concept code.

The Team Behind It: Why $1.5M+ in Bug Bounty Payouts Matters

Open·kritt is not a theoretical research project from an academic lab. It is the open-source distillation of the internal tooling used by the Kritt team (Blockian), a group that has collectively earned over $1,500,000 in bug bounty payouts on platforms like Immunefi and HackenProof. This is a critical distinction: the architecture and workflow philosophy embedded in open·kritt were forged in the crucible of real-world vulnerability hunting against live, high-value targets.

From Internal Tool to Open Source

The Kritt team built open·kritt to solve a problem they experienced firsthand: AI models are powerful at finding vulnerabilities in theory, but raw model output is noisy, unvalidated, and often hallucinated. Their internal system evolved to include validation pipelines, de-duplication logic, and severity ranking — features that are now baked into open·kritt’s core design. By releasing it under the AGPL-3.0 license, they are inviting the security community to build on, extend, and improve the platform.

Track Record as Trust Signal

In the AI security space, trust is everything. A tool that claims to find vulnerabilities is only as credible as the team behind it. The Kritt team’s $1.5M+ payout history on Immunefi and HackenProof — two of the most demanding bug bounty platforms in Web3 and traditional security — provides concrete evidence that the team understands what a real vulnerability looks like and how to validate it. This is not a team of AI researchers who read about security; it is a team of security researchers who learned to build AI tools.

How It Works: Workflow Builder, Scan Execution, and Post-Scripts

Open·kritt’s architecture centers on a workflow-based approach that breaks security research into discrete, manageable steps. This is fundamentally different from the “point AI at whole repo” approach used by many competing tools.

The Workflow Builder

Users define workflows as sequences of tasks. Each task specifies:

  • A model provider (Codex, Claude Code, OpenAI, Anthropic, or OpenRouter)
  • A system prompt that defines the agent’s role and constraints
  • Input context (files, directories, or previous task outputs)
  • Expected output format (structured findings, code patches, or reports)

This modular design means a single workflow might include a reconnaissance agent that maps the attack surface, a scanning agent that probes for specific vulnerability classes, a validation agent that verifies findings, and a reporting agent that generates proof-of-concept code and documentation.

Scan Execution

When a workflow runs, each step is executed by a dedicated AI agent in an isolated Docker container. The agent receives its task, processes the input, and produces structured output. The platform handles:

  • Container lifecycle management — each agent runs in a disposable container that is destroyed after the task completes
  • Output aggregation — results from multiple agents are collected and merged
  • Error handling — failed steps can be retried with different parameters or model providers

Post-Script Validation Pipeline

One of open·kritt’s most distinctive features is its post-script validation pipeline. After an agent produces a finding, a follow-up script can:

  1. Generate a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to confirm the vulnerability is real
  2. Write a structured vulnerability report with reproduction steps
  3. Rank the finding by severity using CVSS scoring
  4. De-duplicate against existing findings in the same session

This validation pipeline directly addresses the central challenge of AI vulnerability hunting: the lab-to-real gap.

Architecture Deep Dive: Docker-Based Self-Hosted Stack

Open·kritt is designed for self-hosted deployment on your own infrastructure. No data leaves your environment, and all AI agent interactions happen inside disposable Docker containers.

Technology Stack

Component Technology
Core language JavaScript (51.2%)
Agent runtime Python (42.2%)
Containerization Docker
License AGPL-3.0
Model providers Codex, Claude Code, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter

Disposable Job Containers

Each workflow step runs in a fresh Docker container that is destroyed after completion. This design provides several security and operational benefits:

  • Isolation — a compromised or hallucinating agent cannot persist on the host
  • Reproducibility — every run starts from a clean state
  • Parallelism — multiple agents can run simultaneously without interference
  • No data leakage — sensitive codebases never leave the Docker host

Model Provider Flexibility

Open·kritt supports five model providers out of the box: Codex, Claude Code, OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter. This flexibility is important for several reasons:

  • Cost optimization — use cheaper models for reconnaissance and expensive models for validation
  • Redundancy — if one provider is down, workflows can fall back to another
  • Benchmarking — compare different models on the same security task to find the best performer
  • Air-gapped deployments — use local models via OpenRouter or self-hosted endpoints

The AI Pentesting Agent Landscape in 2026

The AI security agent space has exploded. As of April 2026, there are 39+ open-source AI pentesting agent projects spanning 6 distinct architecture patterns, and total VC funding in the space exceeds $665M+.

Six Architecture Patterns

Pattern Description Example
Single-agent One LLM handles the entire pentesting pipeline PentestGPT
Multi-agent Multiple specialized agents coordinate on subtasks PentAGI, open·kritt
Specialized roles Agents with fixed roles (recon, exploit, report) open·kritt workflows
Swarm Many agents collaborate without central orchestration Research stage
MCP-based Agents use Model Context Protocol for tool access Emerging
Claude Code native Built on Anthropic’s agentic coding framework Claude Code workflows

Key Benchmark: Multi-Agent Outperforms Single-Agent by 4.3x

The most significant finding from the 2026 landscape survey is that multi-agent hierarchical teams achieve a 4.3x improvement over monolithic single-agent approaches on the HPTSA benchmark for zero-day exploitation. This validates open·kritt’s architectural choice: breaking security research into focused, specialized agent tasks is not just a design preference — it is measurably more effective.

Open·kritt vs Competitors

Feature open·kritt PentAGI XBOW ARTEMIS PentestGPT
Open source Yes (AGPL-3.0) Yes (MIT) No No Yes (GPL)
Multi-agent Yes (workflow-based) Yes (4 sub-agents) Yes Yes No
Self-hosted Yes (Docker) Yes (Docker) No No Yes
Validation pipeline Yes (post-scripts) Limited Yes Yes No
Bug bounty track record $1.5M+ (team) N/A #1 HackerOne N/A N/A
Model provider choice 5 providers OpenAI only Proprietary Proprietary GPT only
GitHub stars 260 (2 days) 14,700+ N/A N/A 6,500+
Release date July 20, 2026 2024 2024 Dec 2025 Late 2023

PentAGI (14,700+ Stars)

PentAGI is the most popular open-source AI pentesting agent, orchestrating 4 sub-agents inside Docker sandboxes. It focuses on the full penetration testing pipeline and has a mature community. However, it is limited to OpenAI models and lacks open·kritt’s flexible workflow builder and post-script validation pipeline.

XBOW (#1 on HackerOne)

XBOW is a commercial autonomous agent that reached #1 on the HackerOne global leaderboard in June 2025, with over 1,060 valid bug bounty submissions. It is the most proven commercial product in the space, but it is closed-source, expensive, and offers no control over prompts, models, or data.

ARTEMIS (Beat 9 of 10 Human Pentesters)

ARTEMIS made headlines in December 2025 by beating 9 out of 10 human pentesters on a live 8,000-host enterprise network, operating at just $18/hour — a fraction of human pentester rates. It is focused on enterprise network pentesting and is not open-source.

PentestGPT (The First Mover)

PentestGPT was the first AI pentesting tool, released in late 2023. It proved that LLMs could reason about attack paths, but it required a human at the keyboard for every command. It is foundational but clunky by modern standards.

The Lab-to-Real Gap: Why Focused Task Decomposition Is the Key Insight

The most important concept in AI vulnerability hunting today is the lab-to-real gap. Research shows that GPT-4 can exploit 87% of one-day CVEs when given advisory descriptions, but only 13% of real CVEs in the CVE-Bench benchmark. That is a staggering 74-point drop.

Why the Gap Exists

The lab-to-real gap exists because:

  1. Advisory descriptions contain hints — when an AI reads a CVE advisory, it knows exactly what to look for
  2. Real codebases are noisy — most code has no vulnerability, and finding the one vulnerable path among thousands of safe ones is fundamentally harder
  3. Context window limits — real codebases are too large to fit in a single model context
  4. Hallucination compounds — a single hallucinated finding in a monolithic scan can waste hours of human review time

How Open·kritt Addresses the Gap

Open·kritt’s workflow-based approach directly addresses each of these problems:

  • Focused tasks — each agent only sees the code relevant to its specific task, reducing noise
  • Validation scripts — every finding is validated with a PoC before it reaches the human reviewer
  • De-duplication — similar findings are merged, reducing review burden
  • Incremental context — agents build understanding incrementally across workflow steps

The 4.3x improvement from multi-agent architectures on the HPTSA benchmark is not theoretical — it is the measured result of this focused task decomposition approach.

Getting Started: Installation and First Scan

Prerequisites

  • Docker installed and running
  • An API key from at least one supported model provider (Codex, Claude Code, OpenAI, Anthropic, or OpenRouter)
  • Git

Installation

git clone https://github.com/Kritt-ai/open-kritt.git
cd open-kritt
cp .env.example .env
# Add your API keys to .env
docker compose up -d

Running Your First Scan

  1. Access the web UI at http://localhost:3000
  2. Create a new workflow using the built-in template library
  3. Point the workflow at a target repository (local or cloned)
  4. Execute the workflow and monitor progress in real-time
  5. Review findings in the results dashboard

The platform includes several pre-built workflow templates for common vulnerability classes including SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), authentication bypass, and smart contract vulnerabilities.

Who Should Use It

Security Researchers

Open·kritt is ideal for professional security researchers and bug bounty hunters who want to:

  • Automate reconnaissance and initial scanning phases
  • Scale their vulnerability research across multiple targets
  • Generate validated PoCs for every finding
  • Build custom workflows for specific vulnerability classes
  • Maintain full control over their data and infrastructure

Security-Minded Developers

For developers who want to audit their own code before release, open·kritt offers:

  • Self-hosted security that never exposes proprietary code to third parties
  • Customizable workflows that match their tech stack
  • Integration with CI/CD pipelines for automated pre-release scanning
  • Clear, validated findings with reproduction steps

Limitations and Considerations

Early Stage

Open·kritt was released on July 20, 2026 — just two days before this review. It has 260 GitHub stars and 51 forks. The community is small, documentation is evolving, and the workflow marketplace is empty. Early adopters will need to invest time in learning the platform and building their own workflows.

Threat Model for Untrusted Code

While open·kritt runs agents in disposable Docker containers, the platform itself is designed for self-hosted use against codebases you control. Running it against untrusted third-party code without additional sandboxing carries risk. The AGPL-3.0 license also has implications for commercial use.

No Built-in Authentication

The current release does not include built-in authentication for the web UI. In a multi-user environment, you will need to put a reverse proxy with authentication in front of it.

Model Costs

While open·kritt itself is free, the API calls to model providers are not. A complex workflow with multiple agents can consume significant tokens, especially when using premium models like Claude Opus or GPT-4 for validation tasks.

The Future: Workflow Marketplace and Community Growth

The open·kritt roadmap includes a workflow marketplace where the community can share, rate, and remix security research workflows. This marketplace could become the platform’s moat: as more researchers contribute workflows for specific vulnerability classes, frameworks, and scenarios, the platform becomes more valuable for everyone.

Other planned features include:

  • Built-in authentication and multi-tenant support
  • Integration with popular bug bounty platforms (Immunefi, HackenProof, HackerOne)
  • Expanded model provider support including local models via Ollama
  • Real-time collaboration for team-based security research
  • CI/CD native integration with GitHub Actions and GitLab CI

Conclusion: A New Paradigm in AI-Assisted Vulnerability Research

Open·kritt represents a new paradigm in AI-assisted vulnerability research. By breaking security research into focused, validated tasks orchestrated across multiple AI agents, it directly addresses the central challenge of the field: the gap between what AI can do in controlled lab settings and what it can achieve against real, noisy codebases.

The team’s $1.5M+ bug bounty track record provides credibility that few open-source security tools can match. The workflow-based architecture is validated by benchmark data showing 4.3x improvement for multi-agent approaches. And the self-hosted, Docker-based deployment model addresses the data sovereignty concerns that prevent many organizations from adopting AI security tools.

Open·kritt is very early — two days old at the time of this review — but the architectural decisions are sound, the team is proven, and the approach is aligned with where the industry is heading. For security researchers who want to experiment with the cutting edge of AI-assisted vulnerability hunting, open·kritt is the most promising open-source option available today.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is open·kritt free to use?

Yes, open·kritt is completely free and open-source under the AGPL-3.0 license. You only pay for the API calls to your chosen AI model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) and the infrastructure to run Docker containers.

How does open·kritt compare to commercial tools like XBOW?

Open·kritt is open-source and self-hosted, giving you full control over prompts, models, and data. XBOW is a closed commercial product that has proven effectiveness (#1 on HackerOne) but costs more and offers no customization. Open·kritt is better for teams that need control; XBOW is better for teams that want a turnkey solution.

Can open·kritt find zero-day vulnerabilities?

Open·kritt’s architecture is designed to find both known vulnerability patterns and novel attack vectors. The multi-agent workflow approach, combined with post-script validation, makes it well-suited for zero-day research. However, like all AI security tools, its effectiveness depends on the quality of the workflows and models used.

What programming languages and frameworks does open·kritt support?

Open·kritt is language-agnostic — it works with any codebase that can be analyzed by the underlying AI models. The platform itself is built with JavaScript (51.2%) and Python (42.2%), and the workflow builder lets you customize prompts for any language, framework, or vulnerability class.

Do I need to be a security expert to use open·kritt?

While open·kritt automates much of the vulnerability hunting process, interpreting results and building effective workflows requires security knowledge. The platform is designed for security researchers and security-minded developers. Beginners should start with pre-built workflow templates and learn from the community as it grows.
